projects.title: Pill Reminder
projects.summary: Pill Reminder is a local-first mobile app for creating medication reminders and keeping a simple daily record of whether a dose was taken, skipped, or missed.
projects.whyBuilt: Medication reminders are often used by people who need an interface to be calm, legible, and dependable. I used the project to explore a deliberately small, offline-capable product where accessibility, privacy, and reliable local notifications are core requirements rather than late additions.

screenshots.alt: Today dashboard with an example reminder

capabilities: Guides a person through language, privacy, and notification-permission setup.
Supports English and Latin American Spanish.
Lets people add, edit, pause, resume, and remove medications.
Creates reminder schedules and a focused today view.
Handles due reminders, including recording whether a dose was taken or skipped and retaining medication history.
Schedules local notifications and offers a settings-based picker for app-bundled reminder tones.
Keeps core data and preferences on-device without requiring an account or a network connection.
technicalHighlights: Local-first design. Medication, schedules, reminder handling, history, setup, and ringtone preferences use focused repositories backed by local preferences.
Reliable notification lifecycle. Scheduling, due-reminder reconciliation, reminder actions, permission status, and ringtone selection are separated into testable services and domain models.
Accessible mobile UX. The product design treats older-adult accessibility as a release requirement, with clear flows, readable type, large touch targets, and localised copy.
Focused Flutter architecture. Presentation, domain logic, persistence, notification services, localisation, and theme code are kept in distinct areas rather than being folded into one screen.
Automated coverage. Unit and widget tests cover medication validation, schedules, today-dashboard behaviour, notification handling, history, setup, settings, and ringtone behaviour.
keyDecisions: The core experience is account-free and offline-capable. This reduces setup burden and keeps medication data private, at the cost of not providing cloud sync.
Notification permission and device settings can override audible reminders, so the application keeps permission status visible and safely falls back to the default sound when needed.
A single global reminder tone avoids turning a simple setting into per-medication configuration.
Android notification channel sounds are immutable after creation; the scheduler therefore uses stable per-sound channel identifiers for selected tones.
projects.status: The application has implemented medication management, schedules, a today dashboard, due-reminder actions, medication history, privacy controls, local notification handling, English/Latin American Spanish support, and ringtone selection. It remains an active mobile project rather than a published medication-management service.

projects.title: Assets Watcher
projects.summary: Assets Watcher is a multi-user stock-portfolio intelligence prototype for tracking US-listed holdings and watchlist ideas. It turns cached market data and transparent, deterministic rules into educational context—not trading instructions.
projects.whyBuilt: I wanted to explore the engineering boundaries of a personal-finance product: user-owned data, scheduled third-party data refreshes, explicit data freshness, and explainable scoring. The product deliberately keeps the decision with the user; its labels and optional AI explanation are informative rather than prescriptive.

screenshots.alt: Dashboard populated with local demo data
Holdings populated with local demo data

capabilities: Authenticates users and creates a default portfolio.
Lets users maintain a cash balance, holdings, and a separate watchlist.
Shows cached company, price, fundamentals, allocation, valuation, quality, safety, and portfolio-fit context.
Makes cached data freshness visible and supports controlled market-data refresh paths rather than fetching on every page render.
Applies deterministic scoring rules with stored, user-scoped score snapshots.
Can generate an on-demand AI take from the app's structured portfolio snapshot, while keeping the deterministic engine as the source of truth.
technicalHighlights: Clear domain boundaries. Market-data providers, scoring, portfolios, holdings, watchlists, authentication, and AI each live behind focused modules.
Safe financial-product language. The scoring model uses cautious labels such as Attractive, Watch, and Avoid / Review; it does not issue buy or sell recommendations.
Protected multi-user data. Supabase Auth, Postgres, row-level security, user-scoped queries, and database migrations model the ownership boundary.

Testable business logic. The repository includes unit and page tests around validation, scoring thresholds, cached-data handling, portfolio calculations, user rules, scheduled refreshes, and provider adapters.
Controlled integrations. Server-only credentials are used for Financial Modeling Prep, scheduled refresh authorization, Supabase administration, and Gemini; the browser does not receive them.
keyDecisions: The app stores and displays cached market snapshots rather than presenting an implied live feed. Freshness states make the limitation explicit.
Deterministic rules are separated from the optional AI explanation, which receives a bounded structured snapshot rather than authority to invent financial facts.
The first scope is intentionally US stocks and manual tracking, which keeps the data model and market-data integration focused.
A full local backend is useful for schema work, but normal browser development can use a hosted Supabase project to avoid a Docker dependency.
projects.status: This is an in-progress prototype. Its authenticated portfolio, holdings, watchlist, stock-detail, scoring, user-rule, cached-market-data, and on-demand AI pathways are implemented in the repository. The wider product roadmap remains in docs/product-plan.md.

projects.title: Pet Seen
projects.summary: Pet Seen is a mobile-first web application for helping people report missing dogs and cats, share privacy-safe public case pages, and submit sightings without creating an account.
projects.whyBuilt: Losing a pet is time-sensitive, emotionally difficult, and location-sensitive. I wanted to design a service that makes reporting and sharing fast without exposing the exact location of a missing animal publicly. The central product constraint is simple: public views are useful, but exact locations remain available only to the case owner and authorised staff.

screenshots.alt: Missing pets near you in list view
Missing pets near you in map view

capabilities: Lets authenticated owners create, edit, share, close, and mark missing-pet cases as reunited.
Generates non-sequential public case URLs that show an approximate, server-provided location area rather than an exact pin.
Lets neighbours submit a location-first sighting without an account, with GPS, place search, movable-pin confirmation, and manual fallback paths.
Gives owners protected access to their case timeline and authorised exact sighting locations.
Includes moderation, found-pet reporting, candidate matching, watch-area alerts, photo processing, poster generation, and multilingual foundations.
technicalHighlights: Privacy-aware geospatial data model. Supabase/Postgres with PostGIS, row-level security, and separate protected and public-safe location data preserve the public/private boundary.
Resilient location UX. MapLibre supports GPS, place search, movable pins, and manual fallback so denied location permission does not block a report.
Feature-oriented React architecture. React Router, TanStack Query, typed Supabase access, focused feature APIs, mutations, and workflows keep page composition separate from data access.

Safe image handling. The upload workflow validates images, strips EXIF metadata, creates private display derivatives, and exposes public images through bounded cacheable URLs only after publication checks.

Controlled assisted matching. Deterministic matching narrows candidates first; AI-assisted scoring is rate- and budget-limited, auditable, and intended for staff review rather than automatic certainty.
Practical quality gates. The project includes unit tests, SQL contracts, end-to-end flows, visual-regression coverage, type checking, linting, and production builds.
keyDecisions: A missing-case owner signs in, but a person reporting a sighting does not need an account. This reduces friction during urgent reporting while retaining a protected owner workspace.
Public exact coordinates are not returned to the client. Approximate locations are generated and persisted server-side for public use.
The initial beta is deliberately restricted to dogs, cats, the United Kingdom, and a focused local launch area.
Photo originals remain private. Public delivery uses processed derivatives and short, bounded cache lifetimes instead of unrestricted storage access.
AI can add operational support, but the system keeps deterministic rules, cost guards, staff review, and safe fallbacks in control.
projects.status: The controlled-beta product is in active development. The delivery plan documents the implemented alpha and beta paths alongside the remaining distribution and follow-up work in docs/PROJECT_BREAKDOWN.md.

projects.title: CitizenShareholders Content Platform
projects.summary: Two content-rich websites for CitizenShareholders: one for the general public and one for investors, both designed to be updated quickly by the client team.
projects.whyBuilt: CitizenShareholders needed two related sites with different audiences, content, imagery, and colour palettes. They needed editorial control quickly, without the time or budget for a bespoke admin panel. As the sole developer, I used WordPress as a familiar content-management layer and built each site as a separate Gatsby frontend.
capabilities: Provides separate public and investor websites, each with its own content, imagery, and publishing workflow.
Lets the client team update website content through the WordPress admin interface instead of depending on a custom-built admin panel.
Applies a shared visual approach across both sites while giving each one distinct primary and accent colours.
technicalHighlights: Built both frontend applications in React with Gatsby.
Configured each WordPress installation as a headless content source, exposing content through JSON endpoints for the corresponding frontend.
Added a WordPress GraphQL extension so each Gatsby site could request only the content it needed instead of retrieving entire endpoint responses.
keyDecisions: Used WordPress rather than a bespoke admin interface to give the client immediate, familiar control over a large volume of editorial content.
Kept the public and investor sites separate because their content and images differed, while using consistent theming techniques to make them clearly part of the same product family.
Exposed GraphQL alongside JSON endpoints to make frontend data queries more focused and efficient.
projects.status: Delivered for CitizenShareholders. The client could manage content independently through WordPress.

projects.title: Ver Análisis
projects.summary: A Spanish-only proof of concept that gives clinics a straightforward way to publish diagnostic reports and lets patients securely open, share, and print them from a unique link.
projects.whyBuilt: Diagnostic reports are often delivered through disconnected channels that make it harder for clinics to keep a consistent identity and for patients to access their results. I built Ver Análisis to explore a small, direct reporting flow: clinicians create a branded clinic, publish a report with its scans, and immediately receive a patient-ready URL and QR code.

screenshots.alt: Patient-facing report with clinic branding, scan thumbnails, sharing, and printing actions
Patient-facing report using a second clinic's logo and colour
Full-screen diagnostic scan viewer with previous and next controls
Doctor workflow for adding a new report
Published report dialog with a QR code and patient-ready URL
Print preview of the patient report
Print preview of the scan image page

capabilities: Lets doctors create clinics with their own logo and brand colour before preparing reports.
Captures the patient details, report content, date, clinician, and scan images in one reporting workflow.
Publishes each completed report with a unique patient URL and a QR code that can be shared through WhatsApp.
Gives patients a Spanish-only report page where they can review scan thumbnails, inspect individual images, share the link, and print a two-page report.
technicalHighlights: Built the proof of concept with React and Tailwind CSS, keeping the doctor workflow and patient-facing report experience in the same web application.
Uses Firebase Firestore for clinic and report data, with Firebase Storage for uploaded diagnostic scan images.
Uses Jest to cover the application behaviour as the reporting workflow evolves.
keyDecisions: Used a unique report code and direct URL so a patient can open a result without navigating a clinic portal.
Made clinic branding configurable at the clinic level, allowing one product to support distinct practices without duplicating the reporting flow.
Kept the patient experience focused on reviewing, sharing, and printing the completed report rather than exposing administrative controls.
projects.status: Proof of concept. The clinician reporting, branded clinic, patient report, image viewing, QR sharing, and print flows are implemented.

projects.title: Luno Buy & Sell Flow Renovation
projects.summary: A frontend-driven renovation of the buy and sell journeys for Luno, a crypto fintech product, making high-stakes transactions clearer and more focused.
projects.whyBuilt: The existing purchase journey had accumulated screens and separated card payment into another browser tab. As the sole web engineer, I rebuilt the experience around a clearer flow that kept customers in context from entering an amount through to confirmation.
capabilities: Guides customers through clearer crypto purchase and sale journeys built from a shared component library.
Reduces the buy journey by two screens by condensing information without removing the context customers need to complete a purchase.
Replaces a four-screen, separate-tab card-payment journey with an in-context modal that closes after confirmed payment and returns the customer to the end-of-flow screen.
Applies the established buy-flow pattern to a sell-flow MVP delivered in about three weeks.
technicalHighlights: Built frontend-driven Angular flows with TypeScript and RxJS, after contributing the required shared components to the company library.
Used an AI-first delivery approach: the buy flow established a reusable example, while the sell MVP was accelerated with Claude Code.
Added analytics, feature flags, and automated coverage with Playwright, Karma, and Jasmine.
keyDecisions: Ran the buy-flow release as an A/B test to validate whether a shorter journey improved the purchase experience; the sell flow reused the proven pattern without a separate experiment.
Kept card payment inside the flow so confirmation returns customers to the right screen instead of losing their context in a separate tab.
Invested in shared components first so the two flows could be assembled consistently and delivered faster.
projects.status: Shipped at Luno. The buy-flow A/B test validated the shorter purchase journey.

projects.title: Luno Dynamic Send & Receive Flows
projects.summary: Backend-driven, country-specific regulatory journeys for sending and receiving crypto, designed to keep Luno compliant with local requirements.
projects.whyBuilt: Send and receive journeys needed to adapt to different local regulations without creating a separate frontend flow for every country. As the sole web engineer, I built a flexible presentation layer that could safely assemble the appropriate journey from backend-provided definitions.
capabilities: Presents compliant send and receive journeys that adapt to country-specific rules.
Builds a Dynamic Flow from backend-provided JSON that identifies the screen type and supplies its content.
Renders either a predefined screen or a generic composition of shared components, depending on the backend definition.
technicalHighlights: Implemented an Angular and TypeScript presentation layer for backend-driven screen definitions, using RxJS to coordinate dynamic state.
Used the company component library to keep dynamically assembled flows consistent with the wider product.
Added analytics, feature flags, and automated coverage with Playwright, Karma, and Jasmine.
keyDecisions: Kept regulatory decision-making in backend definitions so country rules could vary without duplicating frontend journeys.
Used a small set of predefined and generic screen patterns to handle variation while keeping the customer experience consistent.
Made experimentation and observability part of the flow architecture through feature flags and analytics.

projects.title: TechSoup AngularJS to React Modernisation
projects.summary: A staged modernisation of internal applications at TechSoup, a nonprofit technology provider serving organisations worldwide, moving legacy AngularJS experiences to React.
projects.whyBuilt: Internal applications needed a more maintainable frontend foundation and a practical migration path away from AngularJS. As JavaScript lead engineer, I established that foundation before migrating applications one by one, so teams could modernise without a disruptive rewrite programme.
capabilities: Provides a repeatable path for moving internal applications from AngularJS to React.
Modernises styling from plain CSS to Bootstrap and SCSS, making implementation easier to extend and maintain.
Improves and simplifies legacy AngularJS code while applications wait to be migrated.
Supports a gradual, application-by-application migration instead of a high-risk platform rewrite.
technicalHighlights: Led the JavaScript foundation work across React and AngularJS applications.
Introduced Bootstrap, SCSS, and Tailwind CSS tooling to make styling more consistent and practical to develop.
Used Jest to support a safer migration path as individual applications moved to React.
keyDecisions: Established shared styling and code-quality foundations before migrating applications, so each migration built on a more maintainable base.
Improved legacy AngularJS code rather than treating it as untouchable, reducing friction during the transition.
Migrated incrementally to limit delivery risk for internal teams.

projects.title: TechSoup TypeScript Endpoint Library
projects.summary: An internal TypeScript library that gives applications only the endpoint data they need, reducing repeated data trimming and making API consumption easier for development teams.
projects.whyBuilt: Endpoints often returned more data than individual applications needed, leaving teams to repeatedly trim responses and making correct usage harder for junior developers. As JavaScript lead engineer, I created a shared library that made the intended data shape the default.
capabilities: Reduces endpoint responses to the fields requested through the endpoint parameters.
Removes repeated response-trimming work from consuming applications.
Gives developers a simpler, safer way to consume shared endpoint data.
technicalHighlights: Built the internal library in TypeScript with Jest coverage.
Used Rollup to publish CommonJS output for AngularJS applications and ESM output for React applications.
Created one shared endpoint-consumption layer for applications at different stages of the frontend modernisation.
keyDecisions: Applied response selection inside the shared library so consumers received only the data their endpoint parameters requested.
Published both CommonJS and ESM builds to support the existing AngularJS estate alongside newer React applications.
Optimised the library for clear defaults so less-experienced developers could use endpoints without manual response shaping.
